transcript.text: I'd like to go first, because I've uncovered a critical issue during my patent ownership review this week. I confirmed that one of the patents essential to the licensed technology is jointly owned with Helix University. This means we cannot grant exclusivity — and we cannot execute the license — until Helix University provides written consent. I have not circulated this finding beyond the patent file until now, so I wanted to flag it immediately given our Friday deadline.
transcript.speaker: A2

transcript.text: Thank you, Thomas. Before we go further, I need to share something critical on the commercial side. I confirmed with the product business team this week that our approved commercial position is a 6.5% royalty and a $400,000 annual minimum, limited to exclusive use in hospital cardiac monitoring. The team does not approve worldwide exclusivity. I have not yet updated the negotiation summary with this benchmark, but given what Thomas has just raised about the Helix University joint ownership issue, we now have two independent blockers to the exclusivity NovaBio is requesting — one on the patent side and one on the commercial side. We need to address both before this package can be approved.

transcript.text: Thank you, Thomas and Nadia. I need to share a critical export-control issue. After reviewing NovaBio's technical specifications this week, I classified the licensed encryption module as subject to U.S. export controls. The agreement must prohibit sublicensing to embargoed jurisdictions and require export screening before each transfer. The current draft has no export-control language whatsoever, and I have not yet marked up the draft to address this. This is a third blocker that must be resolved before the package can be approved.
